t: #2531 — Make Number of Distinct Characters Equal
o: We may perform exactly one swap of a character from word1 with a character from word2 and need both strings to end up with the same number of distinct characters. Only the *counts* of each letter matter, not positions. In example 1 (`"ac"`, `"b"`) every swap leaves word1 with 2 distinct letters and word2 with 1, so the answer is false. In example 3 every swap keeps 5 and 5, so the answer is true. Since there are only 26 lowercase letters, we can afford to try every pair of letters (a from word1, b from word2) rather than every pair of indices.
k: Only the multiset of characters matters; positions are irrelevant.
Trying all 26×26 letter pairs is enough — a swap of letter a with letter b affects only the counts of a and b.
Whether a letter's distinct-count changes depends only on whether its count hits 0 or rises from 0.

a.i: Keep frequency maps and distinct counts d1, d2 for both words. For each letter a present in word1 and each letter b present in word2 (a != b), simulate swapping one occurrence: word1 loses an a (distinct count drops if cnt1[a]==1) and gains a b (rises if cnt1[b]==0); symmetrically for word2. If any pair equalizes the distinct counts, return true.
s: Build frequency counters and distinct counts for both words.
Double loop over letters a in counter1 and b in counter2, skipping a == b.
Compute the new distinct counts after one swap using the boundary conditions cnt==1 and cnt==0.
Return true if any pair matches; otherwise false.
a.t: O(|word1| + |word2| + 26^2) — building counters is linear, the pair enumeration is constant.
a.sp: O(26) for the two frequency arrays.

w: This constant-factor enumeration is the intended optimal solution; simulating actual index swaps is unnecessary. Pitfalls: forgetting to skip a == b (a swap of identical letters changes nothing), and getting the boundary conditions right (a letter disappears only when its count is exactly 1; a new letter appears only when its count is 0). Follow-ups might ask for the minimum number of swaps, which requires a BFS over count vectors.
